notes:
Here are the research notes on 1 Kings 11:1–22, arranged verse by verse.

---

## v. 1 — Solomon's Foreign Wives

**Traditional Reading**

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic):** Two problems are evident — Solomon loved *foreign* women who worshipped other gods, and he loved *many* women, rejecting God's design of one man–one woman (Gen 2:23–24; Matt 19:4–6). Solomon probably thought he would be the exception to the rule and escape the consequences. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)
- **Gill (Baptist):** His love was "lustful and not a lawful one." The daughter of Pharaoh is distinguished — she was probably a proselyte and had no hand in his idolatry, since no high place is ever mentioned for an Egyptian deity. Solomon's marriages to the other nations may have had political motives ("to get intelligence of the state of those countries") but more likely were "the fruit of lust or pride." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Polygamy at this scale was also practiced by David, but Solomon carried it out "on a scale corresponding to the magnificence of his kingdom" and likely had political objects of alliance with neighbouring or tributary kings. The first three nations (Moab, Ammon, Edom) were kindred to Israel through Abraham; the last two (Sidonians, Hittites) were Canaanite. Only the Canaanites were explicitly forbidden in the Law, but by this time the reason applied equally to all. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry (Puritan/Reformed):** "The love of women has cast down many wounded." David had multiplied wives too much, and perhaps Solomon presumed it was lawful from his father's example. "The way of sin is down-hill." Henry suggests the foreign women "pleased him with the looseness and wantonness of their dress, and air, and conversation." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)

**Modern Scholarship**

- **Peake's Commentary:** A Deuteronomic editor's influence is unmistakable in the present form of the narrative, though the account of Solomon's adversaries (vv. 14ff) comes from an earlier source. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/1-kings-11.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/1-kings-11.html)

---

## v. 2 — The Prohibition and Solomon's Clinging

**Traditional Reading**

- **Guzik:** Solomon "clung to these in love" — for all his wisdom, he was snared by romantic and sensual attraction. He did not consider that "it is possible to be romantically and sensually attracted to people we have no moral or righteous reason to be attracted to." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)
- **Gill:** The prohibition "Ye shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in unto you" refers especially to the Hittites, one of the seven nations covered by Deuteronomy 7:1. "Solomon clave unto these in love" means "he not only took them, but kept them, and expressed a strong affection for them." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** Solomon "was extravagantly fond of them, set his heart upon them, spent his time among them." He "despised Pharaoh's daughter, his rightful wife… in comparison of them." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)
- **StudyLight.org verse-by-verse:** The writer's condemnation rests on Deuteronomy 23:3–9 as well as Deuteronomy 7:3–4. [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/11-1.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/11-1.html)

---

## v. 3 — Seven Hundred Wives and Three Hundred Concubines

**Traditional Reading**

- **Guzik:** "This is an almost unbelievable number." Concubines were legal mistresses — many prominent OT men had them, but "the Bible never shows this kind of family life blessed by God." Solomon followed David's bad example, was driven by sexual lust and lust for power/prestige. "If one wife is not enough to satisfy a man, then 1,000 wives will not be enough." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)
- **Gill:** "A prodigious number; though these might not be all for use, but for state after the manner of the eastern monarchs." This number seems plainly referred to in Ecclesiastes 7:28. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The numbers are "not only extraordinarily large, but excessive" compared with the "threescore queens and fourscore concubines" of Song of Solomon 6:8 and "disproportionate in the relative number of the superior and inferior wives." He suggests "the text may be corrupt, though the corruption must be of ancient date." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** "Not one good one among them," he notes from Ecclesiastes 7:28, "for no woman of established virtue would be one of such a set." Henry links this to Deuteronomy 17:16–17 forbidding kings to multiply horses or wives. [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)

---

## v. 4 — Solomon's Heart Turned in Old Age

**Traditional Reading**

- **Guzik:** Age did not make Solomon wiser — "old age hardened the sinful tendencies that were present in his younger days." The phrase "his heart was not loyal" uses language elsewhere applied positively only to Joshua, Caleb, and David. Solomon is the conspicuous negative case. David spiritually survived having multiple wives; Solomon did not: "David's lack of romantic and sexual restraint hindered him; it destroyed Solomon." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)
- **Ellicott:** The evil influence "belonged to the time of senile feebleness, possibly the premature result of a life of indulgence; for he could not have been very old." His idolatry was probably "the inclination to an eclectic adoption of various forms of faith and worship," the "philosophic spirit, 'holding no creed, but contemplating all.'" It was "the natural fruit of an overweening confidence in his own wisdom." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** "He grew cool and indifferent in his own religion… He left his first love, lost his zeal for God, and did not persevere to the end." His father David "had many faults, but he never neglected the worship of God, nor grew remiss in that, as Solomon did… and there began his apostasy." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)

**Reformed Perspective**

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** Solomon's love for these women "violates God's warning to his people." The key lesson is that "there is no hope for God's people unless a different kind of king arrives on the scene" — Jesus Christ. Solomon "as a sinner with divided loyalties and a propensity to turn away from God" is "all too like us today." Love easily becomes "a false substitute for God's love." [https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/solomons-sin-and-our-sin](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/solomons-sin-and-our-sin)

**Evangelical/Dispensational**

- **Constable:** Solomon "did not abandon Yahweh, but he worshipped the gods of the nations along with Him (syncretism)." His sin was that his heart (affections) went after false gods. "Solomon was noteworthy for his love for God when he began reigning (1 Kings 3:3), but at the end of his reign, love for women characterized him." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-11.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-11.html)

---

## vv. 5–6 — Ashtoreth and Milcom; Solomon's Evil

**Traditional Reading**

- **Ellicott (on Ashtoreth):** The goddess of the Sidonians (Astarte), representing "the receptive and productive… power in Nature," associated with the moon or the planet Venus, called "the queen of heaven" (Jer 44:17, 25). Her name relates to the root behind Greek *aster* and Latin *astrum* (star). The Hebrew vocalisation "Ashtoreth" is a deliberate distortion based on the word for "shame" (Gu zik notes this too). Her worship "was one of chartered license and impurity." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Ellicott (on Milcom/Molech):** Milcom is "probably only a variety of the well-known Molech." The name "Molech" is a general title meaning "king" (as Baal means "lord"). Its worship involved "the horrible sacrifice of children 'passing through the fire'" (Lev 18:21; 20:2). Historically the Carthaginians practiced the same rite, identifying the god with Saturn. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Gill:** Jewish writers (Ben Gersom, Abarbinel) think "he did not worship these idols, but suffered his wives to do it, and connived at it, which was his sin." "He did not wholly, and constantly, and solely serve the Lord, as his father did." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Guzik:** "This seems almost unbelievable… This man of great heritage, wisdom, and blessing turns to the most depraved gods of the pagan nations." Solomon probably thought he still honoured the LORD and simply added these; "but this is never acceptable to God." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

---

## v. 7 — High Places for Chemosh and Molech

**Traditional Reading**

- **Ellicott:** "On the hill that is before Jerusalem" is "evidently on the Mount of Olives (part of which still traditionally bears the name of the 'Mount of Offence'), facing and rivalling the Temple on Mount Moriah." Tophet, where actual child sacrifice to Molech occurred, was "in the valley of the son of Hinnom" (2 Kings 23:10; Jer 7:31), east or south-east of the city at the foot of the mountain. Chemosh probably means "the Conqueror" or "Subjugator," a god of battles; the Moabite Stone refers to "Ashtar-Chemosh." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Gill:** Solomon "ordered to be built, or at least suffered it to be built, at the instigation of his Moabitish woman." The Mount of Olives was called "the mount of corruption" afterwards (2 Kings 23:15). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** Setting up a high place for Chemosh on the mount before Jerusalem was done "as if to confront the temple which he himself had built." These high places remained "not utterly demolished, till Josiah's time" (2 Kings 23:13). [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)
- **Guzik:** "Because of lust, Solomon found himself in a place where he never thought he would find himself… at the altar of child sacrifice unto the god Molech. This is the power of lust – it can capture us in a spell, in a fog of spiritual confusion until we do things we never thought we would do." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

---

## v. 8 — All His Foreign Wives Worshipped Their Gods

**Traditional Reading**

- **Gill:** "When he had done it for one, he could not refuse it to another, without greatly disobliging them." This shows "that the best and wisest of men, when left to themselves, may do the worst and most foolish of all things." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** "When he humoured one thus, the rest would take it ill if he did not, in like manner, gratify them, so that he did it for all his wives." Henry says Solomon "made a jest of it, asking, 'What harm is there in it? Are not all religions alike?' — which (says bishop Patrick) has been the disease of some great wits." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)
- **Expositor's Bible:** "To crown all, Solomon not only showed this guilty complaisance to all his strange wives, but even, sinking into the lowest abyss of apostasy 'burnt incense and sacrificed unto their gods.'" [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-kings-11.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-kings-11.html)

---

## vv. 9–10 — The LORD's Anger and the Two Appearances

**Traditional Reading**

- **Gill:** "The Lord was angry with Solomon" — "or from the fear of him, as the Targum, which must in a great measure be cast off, or he could not have given in to idolatry in any shape." The two appearances were at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:5) and after the dedication of the temple (1 Kings 9:2); mentioned "as an aggravation of his sin." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** "God keeps account of the gracious visits he makes us, whether we do or no, knows how often he has appeared to us and for us, and will remember it against us if we turn from him." His sin was "the most base ingratitude that could be" and "the most wilful disobedience." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)
- **Guzik:** "We sometimes think that great spiritual experiences will keep us from sin and will keep us faithful to God. This was not the case with the wisest man who ever lived." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

---

## vv. 11–13 — The Judgment Announced: Kingdom Torn Away but with Mercy

**Traditional Reading**

- **Gill:** The Lord spoke to Solomon "not in a vision, as before, but by a prophet; the Jews say Ahijah the Shilonite, which is probable" (see v. 29). The "one tribe" refers to Judah (with Benjamin absorbed). "Not for the merits of David, but the promises made to him" (2 Sam 7:12); also "for Jerusalem's sake… to have the house of his sanctuary and worship in." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** The sentence is just: "since he had revolted from God, part of his kingdom should revolt from his family; he had given God's glory to the creature, and therefore God would give his crown to his servant." Yet the mitigations are kind: not in Solomon's lifetime, and not the whole kingdom. "Thus all the favour God shows to man is for Christ's sake, and for the sake of the covenant made with him." Henry also holds out hope of Solomon's repentance: "we have reason to hope that he humbled himself before God… that penitential sermon [Ecclesiastes] was as true an indication of a heart broken for sin… as David's penitential psalms were." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)
- **Pulpit Commentary Homiletics:** The judgment shows God's justice: "Solomon, the servant of God, rebelled against God; Jeroboam, the servant of Solomon, rebels against Solomon." Yet mercy tempers it: delayed for David's sake, and one tribe retained. "David, the beloved, was a type of Christ, for whose sake the entail of infinite mischief is cut off from his sons." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Guzik:** "The true security of Israel did not rest in… wealth, military power, and prestige. It rested in the blessing of God and in the obedience and faithfulness of their king." The "one tribe" reference (though the south held Judah and Benjamin) is "because either Benjamin is swallowed up in Judah, or the idea was one tribe in addition to Judah." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

**Denominational Differences on Solomon's Final State**

- **Enduring Word / Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic):** "The story of Solomon in 1 Kings leads us to believe that he died in apostasy. There is no hopeful or cheerful end to the story in this account." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)
- **Matthew Henry (Puritan/Reformed):** Takes an optimistic view — Solomon likely repented, as evidenced by Ecclesiastes. "Though Solomon fell, he was not utterly cast down… Though God may suffer those whom he loves to fall into sin, he will not suffer them to lie still in it." Yet Henry notes the Holy Ghost "did not think fit expressly to record his recovery, but left it doubtful, for warning to others not to sin upon presumption of repenting." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)
- **Coffman (Church of Christ/Restorationist):** Scholars "are reluctant to face what is written here." He insists the text depicts "total apostasy," rejecting efforts to soften it. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-11.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-11.html)

---

## vv. 14–16 — Hadad the Edomite Adversary and Joab's Slaughter

**Traditional Reading**

- **Guzik:** "Solomon's reign was glorious, but God did not allow it to be completely without problems." Quoting Clarke: "When he sent to Hiram… he could say, There was no Satan [1 Kings 5:4]… but now that he had turned away from God three satans rise up against him at once, Hadad, Rezon, and Jeroboam." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The Hebrew word for "adversary" here is "Satan," which the LXX transliterates. Hadad was "apparently a common name among the Edomite royal family." The war was "one of ruthless extermination." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-14.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-14.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The events in this section "belong, at least in part, to the early years of the reign of Solomon." Hadad and Rezon's resistance "continued through all Solomon's reign… they seem to have become formidable again during his declining years." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Gill:** Joab went "to bury the slain" — Gill notes this as an act of humanity: "it has been always reckoned a piece of humanity to bury the dead of an enemy." He also notes that "cut off every male" was "as he supposed; for it was not fact, since after this they increased again." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch (via Cambridge Bible):** Though the punishment was not to be inflicted till after Solomon's death, "the Lord raised up several adversaries even during his lifetime, which… were to serve as constant reminders that he owed his throne… solely to the mercy, the fidelity, and the long-suffering of God." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-14.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/11-14.htm)

---

## vv. 17–18 — Hadad's Flight through Midian and Paran to Egypt

**Traditional Reading**

- **Gill:** Hadad fled "while Joab was burying the slain… Hadad being yet a little child; whom his father's servants hid." They went through Midian and Paran, "which lay between Edom and Egypt." Taking men from Paran was "either as guides and guards through the wilderness, or to make the better appearance before Pharaoh." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The starting-point "Midian" is curious; if the text is correct, "the reference must be either to some branch of the Midianitish tribes settled between Edom and the desert of Paran, or to a city Midian, not far from the Gulf of Elath." Paran "is part of the Sinaitic region, adjacent to the wilderness of Zin." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)

**Modern Scholarship**

- **Peake's Commentary:** "Two narratives may have been combined, one of an Edomite chief Hadad, and another of a child named Adad." He also asks: "Is it possible that here Egypt (Mizraim) is Musri in N. Arabia?" [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/1-kings-11.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/1-kings-11.html)

---

## vv. 19–20 — Hadad's Favour in Egypt, Marriage, and Son Genubath

**Traditional Reading**

- **Gill:** Hadad "found great favour in the sight of Pharaoh… perhaps for his comely personage, princely qualities, and good behaviour." The name Genubath means "stealth" — possibly "in memory of himself being carried away by stealth from his own land." Queen Tahpenes weaned the child "in Pharaoh's house," indicating extraordinary favour. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Ellicott:** This Pharaoh was probably of the 21st (Tanite) dynasty and was not the same as Solomon's father-in-law. "The intermarriage of Hadad with the royal house, and the inclusion of his son Genubath among the children of Pharaoh, argue an unusual distinction, which could only have been due to a high estimate of the importance of influence over the strong country of Edom." The names Tahpenes and Genubath are "unknown, either in history or in the Egyptian monuments." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** "There he was kindly sheltered and entertained by Pharaoh, as a distressed prince." The weaning "no doubt with the customary festival (comp. Gen 20:18), indicated the admittance of the child into the royal family of Egypt." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)

---

## vv. 21–22 — Hadad's Request to Return

**Traditional Reading**

- **Ellicott:** If Hadad requested to leave on hearing of David and Joab's deaths, "it belongs, of course, to the early part of the reign of Solomon." Pharaoh's "courteous evasion… may probably indicate the beginning of the change of attitude towards the powerful monarchy of Israel." There is likely "some omission or dislocation of the text." The LXX (Vatican MS) adds after v. 22: "and Hadad returned to his land. This is the mischief which Hadad did, and he abhorred Israel, and reigned over Edom." Josephus (Ant. viii.6.6) says Pharaoh initially refused, but in Solomon's declining years permission was granted, and Hadad joined Rezon in Syria. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Gill:** "He wanted nothing at all, had all he could wish for: howbeit, let me go in any wise: he had such an extreme desire to go, that he begged it might not be denied him on any account." Whether Pharaoh knew Hadad's real motive is not stated, "but it is probable he did, and it is certain Pharaoh gave him leave to go." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/11.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** Makes a pious application: "Heaven is our home, and we ought to keep up a holy affection to that, and desire towards it, even when the world, the place of our banishment, smiles most upon us." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM](https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC11011.HTM)
- **Guzik:** "We are not told specifically how Hadad troubled or was an adversary to Solomon, only that he returned to bother Solomon with the permission of Pharaoh." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/)

---

## Summary of Points Where Traditions Differ

1. **Solomon's final salvation (vv. 9–13).** Pentecostal/charismatic commentators (Guzik) lean toward Solomon dying unrepentant. Reformed/Puritan interpreters (Matthew Henry) argue Ecclesiastes shows repentance, though they admit Scripture does not record it explicitly. Church of Christ (Coffman) insists on total apostasy. This reflects wider debates about perseverance of the saints.

2. **Nature of Solomon's idolatry (vv. 4–8).** Older Jewish commentators (cited by Gill) and some Anglicans (Ellicott) view it as syncretism or connivance rather than personal worship. More conservative evangelical commentators (Guzik, Coffman) see active participation, even at Molech's altars.

3. **Textual issues in Hadad's narrative (vv. 14–22).** Modern scholarship (Peake) suggests two combined narratives. The LXX and Josephus offer different arrangements, noted by Ellicott. Traditional commentators generally harmonise.
